Lives · 100–44 BCE

Julius Caesar

Politics & War · Rome · 100–44 BCE

2 min readWhere it is contestedUpdated 19 September 2026
On this pageWhere it is contestedThe definitive biographyReads across to

He turned the Roman Republic into something it could never undo.

If you keep one line

Learn the template so you recognise it: the strongman who claims to rescue the republic he is dismantling.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

A patrician of modest fortune and boundless ambition, Caesar climbed the ladder of Roman politics through debt, charm and audacity. Then he conquered Gaul. The campaign killed or enslaved millions and made him the richest and most dangerous man in Rome.

When the Senate ordered him to disband his army he crossed the Rubicon with a single legion and plunged the Republic into civil war — a phrase that still means a point of no return. Victorious, he ruled as dictator and reformed the calendar we essentially still use. Senators hoping to save the Republic stabbed him to death. They guaranteed its end instead: within a generation his heir Augustus founded the empire that would carry Caesar's own name forward as a title, surviving in “kaiser” and “tsar”.

He was at once a literary stylist, a military genius, a populist reformer and a tyrant. He is the original template for the strongman who claims to rescue a republic he is dismantling.

01Where it is contested

Goldsworthy is the standard popular life, but he is comparatively sympathetic to his subject and light on the Gallic campaign as atrocity. Historians of the late Republic also differ on how far Caesar's ambition, rather than deeper structural failure, actually caused the collapse.

02The definitive biography

Caesar: Life of a ColossusAdrian Goldsworthy · 2006

A military historian by training, Goldsworthy grounds the myth in the realities of Roman politics and warfare — the most complete and readable single-volume life.
